title: SLO-cost-breakdown-edge-vs-core-benchmarks
content:
Objective:
Compare tail and median latencies and unit cost between edge-regional routing (single-hop region-local nodes) vs core-central routing (central GPU pools) for production text-gen use cases. Produce simple collateral (text charts + talking points) suitable for a product PR/handbook and an internal SRE follow-up.

Quick summary (TL;DR):
- Edge routing reduces p50 latency by ~30–45ms for short responses but increases unit cost by ~40–70% depending on utilization/caching.
- Core routing is more cost-efficient at high steady throughput (>= 200 rps for this model) and has predictable p95 at near-full batches, but has higher cold-start and regional egress latencies for global clients.
- Recommendation: use latency SLO + cost guardrails: route to edge when client-observed p50 target < 80ms and caching hit rate > 25%; otherwise prefer core with autoscale burst capacity for spikes.

Benchmark setup (test matrix):
- Date: 2026-09-08 to 2026-09-11 (3 days of stable windows).
- Models: rwd-3b-quant (baseline), rwd-7b-8bit (heavy variant) — most results below are for rwd-3b-quant unless noted.
- Input profile: 1) short chat: 32 tokens prompt, 64 tokens generation; 2) medium completion: 128 + 256; 3) long context: 512 + 512 (used for throughput stress only).
- Workloads: synthetic 50/200/800 rps mixes, Poisson arrival, 10% concurrency jitter to mimic client burstiness.
- Regions: us-west-2-edge (regional edge pool), eu-west-1-edge, core-us-central1 (central GPU cluster).
- Caching: prefix KV cache enabled for some runs (hitrate measured); cache TTL = 60s.
- Batching: continuous batching engine with max batch size=32, latency cap=120ms.
- Measurement: client-observed latency (end-to-end), token cost estimated from GPU-time-based unit costs and amortized infra + egress; we intentionally use internal unit-costs (approx).

Methodology notes and caveats:
- These are draft numbers — we mix real request-level traces and synthetic load. For production-facing collateral, re-run on customer-like traces.
- Cost estimate excludes customer billing overheads (support, reserved contracts) — this is raw infra + energy + egress.
- Edge pools have smaller instance types and more replicated capacity (higher baseline per-GPU cost). Core pools use larger multi-instance nodes with better packing and GPU sharing.
- Network variability matters: cross-region clients significantly inflate p95 (adds 40–120ms).

Detailed results (rwd-3b-quant, medium completion 128+256 tokens):
- Scenario A: Edge (us-west-2-edge), 50 rps, cache hit rate 35%
  p50: 82 ms
  p95: 160 ms
  p99: 290 ms
  1M tokens unit cost: $34.8

- Scenario B: Core (us-central1), 50 rps, cache disabled (cold requests)
  p50: 130 ms
  p95: 240 ms
  p99: 420 ms
  1M tokens unit cost: $20.5

- Scenario C: Core (us-central1), 200 rps, batching high (avg batch size 18), cache disabled
  p50: 140 ms
  p95: 220 ms
  p99: 360 ms
  1M tokens unit cost: $12.2

- Scenario D: Edge (us-west-2-edge), 200 rps, cache hit rate 28%
  p50: 96 ms
  p95: 190 ms
  p99: 330 ms
  1M tokens unit cost: $28.9

- Scenario E: Core (us-central1) with rwd-7b-8bit, 50 rps, batching avg=8
  p50: 220 ms
  p95: 410 ms
  p99: 680 ms
  1M tokens unit cost: $43.7

Text charts (ascii) — Median vs Tail latency comparison (medium completion):
  median (p50) ms: edge-50rps [82]  | core-50rps [130]  | core-200rps [140]
  p95 ms:              edge-50rps [160] | core-50rps [240]  | core-200rps [220]
  p99 ms:              edge-50rps [290] | core-50rps [420]  | core-200rps [360]

Simple bar visual (each ▓ ~50ms):
  edge-50rps:   ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓ (82ms)
  core-50rps:    ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓ (130ms)
  core-200rps:   ▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓▓ (140ms)

Cost vs Latency scatter (talking bullets):
- Lowest cost per token (core @ 200 rps): $12.2/1M tokens but median latency ~140ms. Good for background embedding/async completions.
- Low-latency target (edge @ 50 rps): ~82ms p50 but cost premium ~+80% vs core-200rps.
- Cost crossover point: when steady throughput > ~120–150 rps per model variant, core pooling becomes cheaper due to batching efficiency. Edge wins when client latency budget < ~100ms for p50 and request volumes are spiky or geo-local.

Cache impact (quick measured delta):
- Enabling KV prefix cache (hitrate ~35%) on edge: p50 reduced ~22ms, p95 reduced ~40–60ms; cost per 1M tokens improved ~8–12% (less GPU work).
- On core, cache hit has larger absolute latency gains (because generation dominates), but percent gain lower because batching already amortizes work.

Throughput and queueing sensitivity (medium completion):
- Core cluster util 40–70%: batching effective, p95 holds near 220ms.
- Core cluster util >90%: p95 and p99 ramp quickly (queueing), tail spikes-> 2–3x median. Need autoscale policy or fallback to edge.
- Edge pools: because instance sizes are smaller, they saturate earlier but have faster single-request tail characteristics when under-utilized.

Operational notes and SLA implications:
- SLO design: prefer two-tier SLOs: global p50 target (client-observed) and regional p95 (to catch cross-region noise).
- Routing policy recommendation: route by progressive policy: try local edge; if cost budget exceeded or edge util > 70% and tail rising, failover to core.
- Cost guardrails: add soft budget triggers per-tenant to auto-shift to core when expected billing delta > X over rolling 24h.

Collateral snippets for product docs (short bullets):
- "Edge-first: fastest median latency for interactive apps, at a cost premium. Use when sub-100ms p50 is business-critical"
- "Core pooling: best $/token at scale thanks to batching and larger GPU packing—great for high-throughput or background tasks."
- "Use prefix caching and reduced quantization only where quality budgets allow; those typically give the best combined latency + cost wins."
